Suspected cases must not be counted as confirmed cancers. The Million Women eye analysis, by contrast, concerns incident tumours recorded during follow-up. These case definitions and timings should remain visible in any comparison.

The exposure hypothesis should also identify which tissue is expected to receive the relevant energy. Phone-call duration can be useful as a behavioural measure while saying little about whether a device was near the chest, used hands-free or carried elsewhere between calls. The breast-cancer report includes phone placement questions, but its retrospective design does not turn those answers into measured tissue dose. In the eye-tumour cohort analysis, the number of events and the use categories set another limit on interpretation. Keeping site, dose proxy and study design together prevents a broad headline from outgrowing the data.

modules.title: Start with a confirmed diagnosis

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: The breast-cancer authors report a calling-time association, but the printed group totals conflict with the Methods and screen-time reference coding conflicts with broad prose claims. Its numerical effects remain held pending clarification. The cohort did not find increased eye-tumour risk in its reported phone-use groups. These are different outcomes and populations; one cannot cancel or confirm the other as a generic test of cancer.

modules.title: Describe the actual selected observations

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Daily calling and screen time can correlate with sleep, light exposure, socioeconomic factors and other behaviour. In the breast study they do not isolate absorbed RF dose in breast tissue. Retrospective reporting and control selection are additional concerns. A prospective design reduces some recall problems, but coarse exposure categories and small numbers of uncommon diagnoses can still limit a cohort analysis.

modules.title: Behaviour is not the same as tissue dose

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: An animal cancer experiment can investigate a hazard under controlled conditions; a cell experiment can examine a pathway. Neither directly measures human breast or eye cancer incidence. The NTP and Ramazzini findings therefore need their own exposure and translation assessment. Adding every animal or cellular result to the same human cancer count would misrepresent the independent evidence.

modules.title: Keep experimental endpoints separate

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: NCI provides context on sources, cancer research and exposure measurement. Its distinction between job-title proxies, measured fields and household sources is particularly important here. The current page uses that framework without assigning a new certainty grade or claiming that one agency summary completes a review of every organ, occupation and frequency range.

modules.title: A broad overview is a map, not a verdict

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: The selected studies do not test whether a phone accessory or household shielding programme prevents these cancers. FOPH’s mobile-phone document distinguishes exposure-reduction options from health outcomes and notes that shielding can affect the connection. A genuine prevention claim needs an outcome-specific comparison over a suitable period, with other behavioural changes considered.

modules.title: No general cancer-prevention product is established

overview.text: Cancer sites differ in biology, diagnosis and relevant exposure. NCI’s overview separates household low-frequency fields, wireless RF and occupational settings. A claim about all cancers should not be assembled by combining unrelated outcomes, exposure sources and study designs into a single positive-or-negative total.

The current recovered selection adds a multicentre breast-cancer case-control report and a cohort’s eye-tumour analysis. These are selected leads, not an exhaustive review of every cancer site. Breast-cancer findings need scientific appraisal, and a wider site-specific source search and family reconciliation remain unfinished.

takeaway: The selected breast-cancer report has unresolved group-count and interpretation problems, so its numerical effects are held. The separate eye-tumour cohort analysis does not establish a general cancer effect of EMFs.
title: Other cancers and electromagnetic fields

faqs.a: No. Call frequency can correlate with stress and behaviour, and it is an imperfect measure of absorbed RF exposure.
faqs.q: Does an association with phone calls identify RF as the cause?

faqs.a: Its city and sample counts overlap the fuller Babol report, while date descriptions differ. The relationship remains unresolved and it is not counted as independent confirmation.
faqs.q: Can the infertility letter be counted as another independent study?

intro: Infertility, miscarriage, preterm birth and fetal growth are different outcomes. Exposure proxies and timing are central to each comparison.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: The Babol study compared clinic-defined infertility with controls, using residential proximity to power lines. The two-town pregnancy cohort followed miscarriage while recording fields at outdoor locations. The birth-cohort analysis studied gestational duration, fetal growth and birth weight, and the induction study used reported delivery information. These outcomes require different denominators and observation windows.

modules.title: Outcome definitions and timing matter

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: Babol reported an infertility association with proximity. The miscarriage cohort differed by field metric: front-door averages were not predictive, while maximum alley values were associated. More frequent maternal calling was associated with shorter gestation in a four-cohort analysis, without a fetal-growth or birth-weight association. Some induction-use categories related weakly to preterm delivery, but the authors judged bias and other explanations important.

The four-cohort pregnancy paper is another example of complementary information within established study families. It combines cohort-specific estimates rather than recruiting four new independent replications of every earlier birth-cohort report. The authors note that reported calling could reflect factors such as stress and that some information was collected well after pregnancy. The induction study has a different exposure proxy and its own follow-up and response problems. A reliable overview needs those differences beside the findings; it should not convert the presence of several papers into a single combined estimate of risk from any electrical device.

A retrospective Konya hospital study reported higher listed phone-model SAR among mothers of babies classified as small for gestational age, while recalled daily use-time was similar between growth groups. It assigned SAR from a phone listing rather than measuring maternal or fetal dose. Selection, recall, no reported adjusted causal model and a covariate-table inconsistency limit interpretation. The same-data prediction cutoff is not an independently validated safety threshold.

modules.title: The recovered findings are not one pattern

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Distance is not a personal field measurement. Outdoor readings without activity records do not describe every pregnancy’s dose. Phone-call frequency can reflect stress and other behaviours, and retrospective reporting adds uncertainty. Induction use and medical outcomes were self-reported in an internet panel. These issues affect causal interpretation even when a statistical association is present.

modules.title: Exposure and confounding remain major limits

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: The induction-cooker measurement study helps estimate fields from cooking position and appliance features, but does not show a pregnancy effect. Its fixed-position estimates also require duration information and wider validation. Animal or isolated-cell results would answer separate mechanistic questions and cannot be substituted for human conception or birth outcomes without a justified translation.

modules.title: A measurement model is not an outcome trial

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: FOPH’s induction fact sheet distinguishes measured configurations and limit comparisons from the limited pregnancy literature. HSE’s workplace framework separately considers expectant workers at particular risk, within its UK remit. Neither document makes all home sources equivalent or supplies an individual prediction from one household reading. Formal source appraisal remains necessary for each outcome.

The recovered RF reproductive protocol includes pregnancy and developmental outcomes in experimental mammals exposed in utero. That experimental stream is distinct from observational pregnancy studies in people. Its planned exposure controls and bias assessment describe how evidence would be assessed, rather than a completed conclusion about miscarriage, birth outcomes or human risk.

modules.title: Guidance and clinical outcomes have different scopes

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: These selected reports do not test an EMF product, avoidance programme or household distance rule as a way to improve conception or birth outcomes. Changing a source can alter a physical exposure while leaving the causal and clinical questions unresolved. A useful future study would measure exposure more directly, define outcomes prospectively and account for stress, socioeconomic circumstances and other environmental contributors.

modules.title: No reproductive treatment has been demonstrated

overview.text: This page separates the ability to conceive from outcomes after conception, including miscarriage, gestational duration and birth weight. It also separates phone calling, power-line proximity, residential magnetic-field readings and induction cooking. Those measures do not represent one common dose, even when reports are grouped under “EMF.”

The recovered full texts provide specific observations, with scientific review still pending. Repeated reports from the same clinic or cohort are not automatically independent confirmation. This remains selected-source coverage rather than a completed reproductive systematic review, and the present selection does not resolve every source or pregnancy outcome.

takeaway: The recovered observational reports are mixed and use imperfect exposure measures. They do not establish a general reproductive effect or a proven EMF intervention.
title: Female fertility, pregnancy and EMFs

faqs.a: No. Its size, duration, location, cause and clinical consequences matter; physiological variation is not automatically harm.
faqs.q: Does any temperature change mean injury?

faqs.a: No. It concerns a short, controlled low-field experiment and superficial skin outcomes in healthy adults.
faqs.q: Does the 26 GHz result prove every RF exposure is non-thermal?

intro: Heating is a physical interaction with a dose, time and tissue context. A measured temperature change and a harmful thermal injury are different endpoints.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: Skin temperature, core temperature, local tissue absorption, perceived warmth and a diagnosed burn are not interchangeable. A superficial infrared image may detect one pattern while saying little about another tissue. The 26 GHz experiment explicitly limits its conclusions to monitored skin measures in healthy young adults under controlled conditions, rather than validating every guideline threshold.

Measurement resolution also defines what a negative thermal finding means. The 26 GHz authors discuss their sample, monitoring interval and restriction to superficial sites as limitations. Their conclusion is about changes detectable with that protocol, rather than an assertion that every tissue was continuously measured or that arbitrarily small differences were excluded. In workplace reports, perceived warmth and a medical examination are different observations again. A table should identify the instrument or ascertainment method and exposure duration alongside the endpoint. That information lets the reader distinguish a physical measurement, a subjective sensation and a clinically significant injury.

modules.title: Choose a thermal endpoint before interpreting it

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: The acute 26 GHz study did not detect a consistent skin-temperature response at its tested low fields; temperatures also changed over time during sham sessions. A pooled regional-analysis label differs between prose and Table 1, so every analysis cannot simply be called null. At the other end of the exposure spectrum, the occupational review describes suspected overexposure and repair accidents. These are useful observations within their respective conditions, not contradictory results that can be averaged into one heating score.

modules.title: The dose and scenario determine applicability

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Ambient conditions, movement, clothing and normal thermoregulation can change measured temperatures. The controlled study used matched exposure and sham sessions to distinguish an RF-related effect from changes over time. In everyday settings, warmth from an electronic product’s battery or surface is also a different pathway from RF absorbed in tissue; the exposure method must isolate what is being tested.

modules.title: Temperature has many ordinary influences

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: The experiment used a blinded randomized crossover design with infrared monitoring during brief genuine and sham sessions. That strengthens the specific comparison, but its small healthy-adult sample, acute duration and superficial measures limit transfer to children, impaired thermoregulation or prolonged exposure. A null result under those conditions is narrower than proof that RF cannot produce heating.

modules.title: What the controlled study can establish

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: ICNIRP distinguishes external reference levels from basic restrictions on absorbed quantities and uses frequency-, body-region- and duration-specific assessment. FDA’s oven explanation gives a practical example: microwave energy deliberately heats food inside an enclosure, while outside leakage and thermal burns require separate consideration. A product’s cooking output cannot be substituted for a person’s absorbed dose.

modules.title: Limits use specific quantities and averaging

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: Workplace controls address defined equipment, tasks and established hazards, including maintenance situations that can bypass normal safeguards. That purpose should not be confused with evidence that lowering an already low environmental reading improves sleep, fertility or cancer outcomes. Such benefits require their own comparative studies; the selected thermal sources do not demonstrate them.

modules.title: Preventing overexposure is different from proving a chronic benefit

overview.text: RF energy absorbed in tissue can become heat, and ICNIRP’s explanation ties established adverse heating to dose, duration and the body region involved. This differs from the low-frequency framework of induced electric fields and stimulation. A generic meter reading cannot identify either an internal temperature change or an injury.

The recovered controlled experiment measured superficial skin temperature during a defined 26 GHz exposure and sham condition. A separate thermal-mechanism report carries an unresolved correction signal and is held from this page’s findings. Occupational accidents and ordinary environmental exposures are presented as distinct scenarios. Scientific review is pending.

takeaway: RF can heat tissue at sufficient exposure. The recovered acute 26 GHz experiment found no consistent skin-temperature response under its tested conditions. A pooled-analysis discrepancy remains unresolved, and this does not settle every thermal scenario.
title: Heating and electromagnetic exposure

faqs.a: No. The cited comparison was cross-sectional, and its phone-use measures did not show a tinnitus association.
faqs.q: Does an association with EHS prove that fields caused tinnitus?

faqs.a: No. It concerns the call-time measures, population and follow-up studied, not every RF source or all aspects of device use.
faqs.q: Is a call-time null result proof about every device and sound exposure?

intro: Tinnitus is a symptom, not a field measurement or a tumour diagnosis. Phone use, perceived sensitivity and acoustic exposure need separate consideration.

modules.label: Measurement

paragraphs.text: The Regensburg study assessed tinnitus occurrence and severity using questionnaires; COSMOS also relied on later self-reported hearing symptoms. Self-report is relevant to the symptom experience, but can miss differences in onset, persistence or severity. A tinnitus questionnaire is not a diagnosis of acoustic neuroma and should not be counted as a brain-tumour outcome.

modules.title: Record occurrence, timing and severity

modules.label: Evidence

paragraphs.text: COSMOS did not find an association between baseline call time and tinnitus or hearing loss. The smaller EHS comparison found tinnitus more common in the self-described EHS group, but phone-use measures did not show a tinnitus relationship. Its proposed shared vulnerability mechanism was a hypothesis, not something established by those cross-sectional associations.

The timing in COSMOS is useful because recorded calls preceded the follow-up symptoms, but the record covered a limited baseline period. It was not continuous tracking of every participant’s later phone use. The smaller EHS study’s matched surroundings were intended as rough exposure proxies, not a direct dosimetry programme. Their null phone-use results and their different positive or negative symptom associations should therefore remain tied to the measured variables. A broader review would need to examine hearing-related factors, symptom definitions and changes in device use without assuming that a symptom report identifies the energy source responsible.

modules.title: What the selected studies found

modules.label: Confounding

paragraphs.text: Call time does not perfectly represent absorbed RF, especially across networks and hands-free use. It also fails to describe every sound or behavioural exposure associated with a device. COSMOS used a short baseline record and symptoms at later follow-up, while the EHS study used rough environmental matching and self-report. These limitations constrain inference about a particular causal agent.

modules.title: Phone behaviour is a bundle of exposures

modules.label: Controlled studies

paragraphs.text: The recovered tinnitus papers do not provide a blinded intervention showing that a specified RF exposure triggers tinnitus. Prospective follow-up improves the timing of exposure measurement relative to outcome but remains observational. The cross-sectional EHS comparison cannot establish which condition came first, so its correlation should not become a direct exposure challenge result.

modules.title: Blinding and follow-up answer different questions

modules.label: Agency assessments

paragraphs.text: WHO’s historical EHS fact sheet recognizes that symptoms can be real and disabling while distinguishing symptom experience from attribution to EMF. It is not a current tinnitus-specific review or a diagnostic test for a person’s symptoms. That distinction supports careful investigation without treating a reported sensitivity label as a measured exposure mechanism.

modules.title: Take symptoms seriously while testing attribution

modules.label: Interventions

paragraphs.text: The selected evidence does not show that an EMF shield, avoidance programme or phone accessory treats tinnitus. A change in device use can also change sound, sleep routines, stress and expectations. A credible intervention study would compare a defined treatment, specify relevant outcomes and account for those factors rather than infer an RF effect from improvement after several changes at once.

modules.title: Improvement does not isolate the active change

overview.text: A tinnitus study should specify what participants were asked, whether symptoms were already present and when exposure information was collected. Operator-recorded call time, subjective electromagnetic sensitivity and a measured RF dose are different variables. They cannot be substituted for each other just because all appear in a discussion of phones.

The two recovered reports illustrate that distinction. COSMOS related baseline calling records to later symptoms, while the Regensburg comparison studied people reporting EHS and matched controls at one time. Their populations and designs differ, and related cohort reports do not represent new independent participants. Scientific review remains pending.

takeaway: The recovered COSMOS follow-up found no call-time association with tinnitus. A smaller cross-sectional study linked tinnitus with reported EHS, without establishing fields as the cause.
title: Tinnitus and electromagnetic fields
